title: The decree
hook: all things happen by Allah's knowledge and will, the good and the hard

segments.voice: Yesterday, akhirah, and your line: the last day. Did you do one good thing small enough to weigh as an atom? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-nine.

A bus pulls away just as you reach the stop. A test result comes back. A call with good news, a call with bad. Moments like those can come with a ready-made sentence, and it often starts with if only. If only I'd left five minutes earlier. If only I'd said something. A hadith in Sahih Muslim takes that phrase head on. When something befalls you, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says, don't say if only I had done this. Say: Allah decreed it, and He did what He willed. For if only, he says, opens the door to Satan's work. The sixth article of faith lives right inside that if only.
screen: `A BUS PULLS AWAY.` → `IF ONLY…` → `ALLAH DECREED IT.`

segments.voice: The word is qadar, decree, measure. In the hadith of Jibril, the list of six ends with it: to believe in the decree, its good and its harm. First, the measure. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation, "Lo! We have created every thing by measure." Nothing is random to Allah's knowledge: what happens is known and willed, the easy days and the hard ones. Second, what the belief is for. In another passage, the Qur'an says what is coming is already written, so that a person doesn't despair over what slipped away or get carried away by what was given. Qadar steadies both ends: the loss and the win. That's the work the hadith about if only is doing. It doesn't say the bus didn't matter. It says the endless replay doesn't help. Third, what it doesn't mean. There's another hadith, in Tirmidhi's collection, where a man asks whether to tie his camel or leave it loose and trust Allah. The answer: tie it, and trust. Decree isn't permission to stop trying. A person still plans, works, takes medicine, ties the camel. Fourth, the open question. How Allah's decree and human choice fit together is an old argument in Islamic theology, and Muslim schools answer it differently. This path meets those theologians soon. And that completes the six for the week: Allah, the angels, the books, the messengers, the Last Day, and the decree.
screen: `EVERY THING BY MEASURE.` · `NO DESPAIR, NO GLOATING.` · `TIE YOUR CAMEL, AND TRUST.` · then, large: `DECREE AND CHOICE: AN OPEN QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The practice: accept one thing you can't change. Find one if only that's been replaying lately. Not the biggest one; a medium one will do. Notice the sentence your mind keeps saying about it. Then, gently, let the if only go, and just say what happened, plainly, once. It happened. If you pray, you can use the words from the hadith: Allah decreed it, and He did what He willed. If you don't, it happened is enough. Then notice what's still yours to do next. The bell holds the time.
Qadar. Decree, measure: belief that all things happen by Allah's knowledge and will, the good and the hard. The sixth article of faith. Today's word.

Your line: all by his decree. Today, the next time if only starts, swap it for it happened, and then ask what you can do now. This week, six to believe; tomorrow, how faith rises and falls. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Belief in qadar, the divine decree, is the sixth article of faith; when something hard happens, Muslims may say that Allah decreed it, and the advice to tie your camel and trust is quoted alongside it.

fork.setup: you've ridden a camel to meet the Prophet. do you leave it untied and trust Allah to keep it there?
options: tie it, and don't bother trusting.
fork.reveal: in the hadith in Tirmidhi, the answer is tie it and trust. decree in Islam sits alongside effort, not in place of it.
